Wales: A Motorcyclist's Paradise

Wales punches far above its weight for motorcycle touring. Despite its compact size, it contains mountain passes that rival the Alps, coastal roads of stunning beauty, and valley roads that flow like a racing line drawn on the landscape. Here are the roads every rider should experience.

A4069 Black Mountain Pass

The star of many a YouTube riding video and arguably the most exciting biking road in the UK. The A4069 climbs from the Amman Valley over the Black Mountain in the western Brecon Beacons, with sweeping curves, dramatic moorland, and not a speed camera in sight.

  • Distance: 16 miles
  • Surface: Generally good, but watch for gravel and sheep on the upper sections
  • Highlights: The sweeping descent on the southern side, views across to the Beacons, the feeling of total isolation at the summit

A470 Through Snowdonia

The A470 runs the entire length of Wales, but the section through Snowdonia from Dolgellau to Betws-y-Coed is the crown jewel. It passes through ancient oak woodland, alongside rivers, and beneath the mountain massifs of Cadair Idris and the Rhinogydd.

Abergwesyn Mountain Road (Devil's Staircase)

This unnamed road from Tregaron to Llanwrtyd Wells crosses the Cambrian Mountains through some of the emptiest landscape in Wales. The Devil's Staircase section — a series of tight switchbacks climbing steeply through a narrow valley — is exhilarating.

  • Distance: 20 miles
  • Surface: Narrow, sometimes rough. Not for wide touring bikes.
  • Highlights: Devil's Staircase hairpins, Llyn Brianne reservoir, total absence of other traffic

Llanberis Pass (A4086)

The road between Llanberis and Pen-y-Pass, climbing into the heart of Snowdonia beneath the towering crags of Snowdon's east face. Tight, technical, and absolutely spectacular.

A487 Coastal Road (Aberystwyth to Machynlleth)

This coastal stretch follows Cardigan Bay with sweeping views across to the Llŷn Peninsula. The road combines flowing bends with sea views and passes through charming Welsh market towns.

Horseshoe Pass (A542)

Near Llangollen in North Wales, the Horseshoe Pass is a popular biker road with sweeping curves climbing through limestone escarpments. The views from the summit across the Vale of Llangollen are magnificent.

A44 Rhayader to Aberystwyth

A flowing cross-country road through the Cambrian Mountains. Fast, sweeping, and incredibly scenic — it passes through the Elan Valley with its chain of Victorian reservoirs surrounded by hills.

Wales is motorcycle touring concentrated. You can ride five world-class mountain passes and a stunning coastal road all in a single day. The distances are short, the roads are extraordinary, and the riding is non-stop entertainment.

Essential Welsh Riding Tips

  • Many of the best Welsh roads are single-track in places — ride with care and respect passing places
  • Sheep are everywhere and have zero road sense. Slow down near livestock, especially in spring.
  • Welsh weather is wet — the western mountains get enormous rainfall. Carry waterproofs.
  • Fuel stations thin out in mid-Wales. Fill up in towns like Machynlleth, Dolgellau, Rhayader, and Llanidloes.
  • The roads between Snowdonia and the Brecon Beacons are often overlooked — don't skip mid-Wales, it contains some of the best riding in Britain.

If you've never toured Wales on a motorcycle, you're missing one of Europe's great riding destinations. Compact, varied, and packed with exceptional roads — it deserves a place on every touring rider's bucket list.

Essential Lake District Stops

Keswick is the ideal base for Lake District motorcycle touring. The town has good parking, fuel, plenty of cafes and pubs, and sits at the intersection of several major riding routes. The lakeside walk around Derwentwater is a perfect evening activity after a day in the saddle.

Ambleside and Windermere offer more facilities but are busier. For a quieter base, consider Penrith on the eastern edge — it's well-connected by the A66 and gives quick access to Ullswater and the northern fells without the tourist congestion of the central Lakes.

The Ravenglass and Eskdale miniature railway runs through Eskdale — the valley between Hardknott Pass and the coast. If you're passing through, it's worth a short ride on the tiny train for a completely different perspective on the valley you've just ridden through.

Local Knowledge

The Lake District is compact — no point is more than 30 miles from another. This means you can easily change plans mid-ride if weather or traffic makes one route less appealing. Local knowledge says: ride the western fells for solitude, the central fells for drama, and the eastern fells for the best roads. Hawkshead, Coniston, and Boot are charming villages that see less traffic than the main tourist centres. For food, the Drunken Duck Inn near Ambleside serves its own brewery ales with excellent food. The Borrowdale Gates Hotel is a popular biker stop with views across Derwentwater and secure parking. If rain arrives, the Pencil Museum in Keswick and the Wordsworth Museum in Grasmere are atmospheric wet-weather diversions.
keyTakeaways: The A4069 Black Mountain Pass is arguably the UK's most exciting biking road, with sweeping curves and no speed cameras.
You can link five world-class mountain passes and a coastal road in a single day thanks to Wales's compact size.
The Abergwesyn Mountain Road (Devil's Staircase) offers tight switchbacks and near-total solitude, but is too narrow for wide touring bikes.
Mid-Wales roads like the A44 through the Elan Valley are often overlooked yet among Britain's best.
Welsh weather is wet and sheep are everywhere, so carry waterproofs and slow down near livestock.

faq.q: Why is the A4069 Black Mountain Pass so popular with riders?
faq.a: The A4069 combines wide, well-sighted sweeping bends with dramatic open moorland and a genuine sense of isolation at the summit, all without speed cameras. The southern descent flows beautifully and is a favourite in riding videos. Watch for gravel washed onto the upper sections and sheep on the tarmac, and ride it early to avoid slower traffic.

faq.q: Can I really ride several Welsh passes in one day?
faq.a: Yes. Wales is compact, so a single day can link the Horseshoe Pass, Snowdonia passes, the coast at Aberystwyth, Devil's Bridge, the Black Mountain Pass, and Gospel Pass. Distances between highlights are short, which keeps the riding constantly engaging. Fuel up in towns like Machynlleth, Dolgellau, and Rhayader, because stations thin out badly in mid-Wales.

faq.q: Is the Devil's Staircase suitable for a large touring bike?
faq.a: Not ideally. The Abergwesyn Mountain Road is narrow, sometimes rough, and features steep, tight switchbacks that punish wide bars and heavy machines. It suits smaller adventure and naked bikes ridden solo. The reward is the Llyn Brianne reservoir, the switchbacks themselves, and an almost total absence of other traffic through the Cambrian Mountains.

faq.q: When is the best time to tour Wales by motorcycle?
faq.a: Late spring through early autumn offers the best balance of daylight and weather, though the western mountains catch enormous rainfall year-round so waterproofs are essential whenever you go. Spring brings lambs onto the roads, so slow down near livestock. Midweek riding avoids weekend crowds on honeypots like the Llanberis Pass and Pen-y-Pass car park.

faq.q: Which area should I not skip?
faq.a: Do not overlook mid-Wales. The roads between Snowdonia and the Brecon Beacons, including the A44 through the Elan Valley and the A470 corridor, contain some of the finest and quietest riding in Britain. Most tourists head straight for Snowdonia, leaving the Cambrian Mountains gloriously empty and rewarding for riders who make the effort.
